atoms.anchor: Spatial limitations constrain the scope of the preliminary presentation.
The preliminary paragraphs present only an extremely limited subset of a very complex subject.
Only a few general topics pertinent to the following lessons are considered in the preliminary presentation.
Less general linguistic concepts are deferred until the specific grammatical problems to which they apply are discussed.
Languages differ from one another.
Languages can vary widely even when they belong to the same language family.
English is presented as a member of the Indo-European language family.
Russian is presented as a member of the Indo-European language family.
Irish is presented as a member of the Indo-European language family.
Spanish is presented as a member of the Indo-European language family.
Rumanian is presented as a member of the Indo-European language family.
Hindi is presented as a member of the Indo-European language family.
Languages from different families can display still greater differences than languages within one family.
English, Swahili, Tagalog, Arabic, Japanese, Turkish, Quechua, and Nahuatl are listed to illustrate comparison across different language families.
Language diversity is supported by arbitrariness, creativity, and change.
Linguistic arbitrariness means that the content dimension is not motivatedly linked to the medium dimension.
Linguistic creativity means that every language can produce an indefinitely large number of sentences.
Linguistic change means that languages continually change in pronunciation, grammar, and lexicon.
Young children have no problem with language difference.
Young children can apparently acquire native competence in a foreign language as easily as in their first language.
The openness to foreign-language learning described in §1.2 is said to diminish gradually with age.
The openness to foreign-language learning described in §1.2 is said to become lost during the early teenage years.
The loss of early language-learning openness is presented as a reason adults experience linguistic foreignness as a formidable difficulty.
Adult learners have lost much of the linguistic flexibility attributed to children.
Adult learners have lost much of the linguistic receptivity attributed to children.
Acquired habits constrain an adult learner's response to a foreign language.
Acquired presuppositions constrain an adult learner's response to a foreign language.
Acquired predispositions constrain an adult learner's response to a foreign language.
These habits, presuppositions, and predispositions operate as automatic expectations and responses.
The constraining expectations and responses are inculcated during the learner's formative years.
Andrews argues that an adult learns a foreign language partly by using the adult’s own language as a means of comparison.
Andrews argues that an adult learns a foreign language in constant struggle against interference from the adult’s own language.
A native speaker’s ease in handling minute details of pronunciation results from years of intimate familiarity.
A native speaker’s confidence in handling subtle details of thought expression results from years of intimate familiarity.
The author calls native familiarity ‘innocent’ when the mind is unaware of language-transfer pressure.
An adult foreign-language learner does not have the years of intimate familiarity available to a native-learning child.
An adult foreign-language learner does not have the child's innocence of language-transfer pressure.
An adult foreign-language learner must use an acquisition strategy different from a child's strategy.
An adult learner should compensate for limited time through alert, thoughtful, repetitive practice of basic patterns.
Language learning resembles other skills in requiring attentive repetition of basics to achieve familiarity and ease of performance.
An adult learner should offset reduced learning innocence by using the adult advantage of intellect.
Adult language learning should employ comparative reasoning.
Adult language learning should employ contrastive analysis.
An adult language learner should accept the assistance of grammatical explanation.
Grammar is a reasoned description of a language's elements and the rules governing relationships among those elements.
Technical terminology is necessary in grammatical study.
Technical terminology can be a stumbling block in grammatical study.
Technical terminology can strongly discourage or mentally disengage a learner.
The learning objective addressed by this grammar extends beyond superficial, make-do conversational knowledge.
A learner pursuing that objective must overcome antagonism to grammar and grammatical terminology.
Language transfer is distortion imposed on a foreign language through the influence of the learner's native language.
An adult learner needs conscious reasoning to offset language-transfer effects.
Grammatical terms function as technical tools for conscious reasoning about language.
The author argues that grammar is needed to enter the system that generates a foreign language’s morphological peculiarities.
The author argues that grammar is needed to enter the system that generates a foreign language’s syntactic peculiarities.
The author rejects studying examples alone as sufficient for learning a foreign language’s structure.
Without grammatical explanation, a learner will tend to distort a foreign structure by interpreting it through the structure of the learner's own language.
The grammar of a translation equivalent can insidiously replace the grammar of the language being analyzed.
Spanish se leen los libros can be translated ‘one reads the books.’
An uninformed translation-based analysis may incorrectly treat se in se leen los libros as a subject meaning ‘one.’
In the analysis presented here, se in se leen los libros is a direct object meaning ‘themselves.’
Translation-based misconstruals may permit practical communication, but they obstruct access to the foreign language’s own conceptual patterns.
Retraining oneself away from misconceptions motivated by translation is described as especially difficult.
Unfortunately, however, grammars are not always trustworthy guides.
Andrews attributes some untrustworthy grammatical descriptions to linguicentrism among grammarians and linguists.
Linguicentrism or glottocentrism is the belief that one's own language is the measure of language generally.
Learners who treat their own language as the measure of language may impose its grammar on a foreign language.
Some grammarians describe the grammar of a translation as though it were the grammar of the source language itself.
Some analysts invent explanations that make a foreign language appear to comply with the grammar of their own language.
The examples following §1.3 are presented to illustrate translation-centered analytical practices relevant to studying Nahuatl.
Andrews analyzes the relevant Spanish subject affixes as affixal subject pronouns.
Andrews criticizes the analysis of those Spanish affixes as mere subject markers because it denies their pronominal status.

When reading an unannotated Nahuatl causative transform, the reader must consider multiple possible sources before selecting the contextually appropriate translation.

For example, tinečtēcaquitiltia may be generated either by nictēcaquitia, “I inform s.o. of it,” or by nicaquitilo, “I am informed of it,” and therefore may be translated as “you have me inform s.o. of it” or “you have s.o. inform me of it.”
Similarly, tinčtēchnōtżaltia can be generated by either nitēnōtza, “I call s.o.,” or ninōtzalo, “I am called,” and therefore may be translated as “you have me call s.o.” or “you have s.o. call me.”
In all likelihood the general context will decide the choice that should be made
The reader must learn to recognize the possible source analyses in order to use context properly when resolving a multiple-object causative transform.

There are five basic kinds of patientive nounstems, each determined by the nature of the source VNC core.
A passive core can serve as the source of a patientive nounstem.
An impersonal core can serve as the source of a patientive nounstem.
A perfective active core can serve as the source of a patientive nounstem.
An imperfective active core can serve as the source of a patientive nounstem.
A verb root or stock can serve as the source of a patientive nounstem.
A passive core is built on a nonactive verbstem and is distinguished by the nonspecific object pronoun or pronouns appropriate to a passive VNC.
An impersonal core is built on a nonactive verbstem and is distinguished by the nonspecific object pronoun or pronouns appropriate to an impersonal VNC.
Lessons 21 and 22 are cited for the nonspecific object pronouns appropriate to passive and impersonal VNCs.
In serving as a source for a nounstem, the nonactive stem in the passive or impersonal core is truncated in one way or another.
When the nonactive suffix is lō, the nounstem is created by deleting the final /o:/.
An /i/ immediately preceding the /l/ left by lō-truncation is always long.
An /o/ immediately preceding the /l/ left by lō-truncation is always long.
An /a/ immediately preceding the /l/ left by lō-truncation has reduced-long pronunciation.
Reduced-long /a/ before the /l/ left by lō-truncation is spelled without a macron.
If the nonactive suffix is lo-hua, both the hua and the ō are deleted.
When the nonactive suffix is o or o-hua, the derived nounstem deletes the entire suffix.
In all these instances the derived nounstem belongs to the tli class.
When the nonactive suffix is hua, the patientive nounstem is created by deleting the hua.
Such a nounstem belongs to the ti class.
Due to the many idiosyncrasies in the formation of patientive nounstems, no exact rules can be given.

In an agentive NNC, the subject pronoun represents the entity about which the agentive predicate makes its assertion.
An agentive NNC can assert that its subject entity has reached a certain condition.
An agentive NNC can assert that its subject entity customarily performs an action.
An agentive NNC can assert that its subject entity has performed an action.

Nahuatl place-names are structured as NNCs.
Translations may omit explicit representation of the NNC structure of Nahuatl place-names.
English translations supply whatever preposition English requires for the relevant place relation.
An English preposition chosen in translation does not constitute a Nahuatl preposition or determine the Nahuatl structure.
The translation of many Nahuatl place-name NNCs is conjectural; some are open to various interpretations; some are opaque.

A group of adverbialized NNCs functions as modifiers of adverbial modifiers.
A group of adverbialized VNCs functions as modifiers of adverbial modifiers.
This group is among the most frequent adverbial modifiers of adverbial modifiers.
Members of this group are called intensifiers.
Intensifiers are also called qualifiers.
In addition to being able to perform normal adverbial functions, the members of this group have the special capability of intensifying the meaning…
In this function the adverbial modifier always precedes its head.
When functioning as an intensifier
When functioning as an intensifier, an adverbial nuclear clause may have a special translation value.
The following are a few of the most common intensifiers:

An interrogative adverbial NNC must appear sentence-initially in order to retain interrogative status.
Obligatory sentence-initial placement tends to upgrade an interrogative adverbial adjunct to principal-clause rank.
When the interrogative adverbial adjunct is upgraded, the original principal clause tends to be downgraded to adjunct rank.
The clause-rank reversal accounts for the frequent adjunctor in after an interrogative adverbial NNC.
Traditional solid writing of adjunctor in with the interrogative NNC obscures the syntactic relationship.
The Canvas transcription writes in separately whenever an adjoined clause is present.
Section 43.4 is cited for comparison with the interrogative pronominal NNCs tleh and āc.
Traditionally, the adjunctor in is written solid with the interrogative NNC.
Writing the adjunctor in solid with the interrogative NNC is criticized as obscuring the syntactic relationships.
whenever an adjoined clause is present

Quēn is, of course, an exception ( quē in is never found).

Ōquicac in quēn in huetzi in īnnāhuafīl in tlequiquixtli is a witnessed perception clause with an embedded manner proposition.
The zero subject of ōquicac identifies a third-person singular human hearer in the stated 'he' reading.

In quēn introduces the manner or way in which the embedded event occurred: 'how.'
In tlequiquixtli identifies the nonhuman firetrumpet or gun as the singular subject of huetzi.

Īnnāhuafīl specifies a plural human source whose order governs the discharge: 'at their order.'

Structures of adverbial modification can be more complicated than those presented in Lesson 49.
In Lesson 49, an adverbial modifier may be an adverbialized nuclear clause whose subject pronoun is adverbialized.
In Lesson 49, an adverbial modifier may instead be an adverbial unit headed by an adverbialized nuclear clause.
In the structures of adverbial modification presented in this lesson, the adverbial modifier is not adverbialized
it is merely an adjoined clause (or clause unit) that may or may not contain an explicit indication (i.e., an adjoined adverbialized NNC) of the nature of the adverbial modification.
There are ten meaning types, which will be taken up in the following paragraphs.
The principal clause unit is modified by an adverbial clause unit that has a temporal meaning.
The temporal meaning may be implicit, with the adjoined clause unit containing no time-indicating NNC:
Ye ōnitlacuah in ōahcico. is a witnessed temporal adverbial-clause construction.
Ni- in ōnitlacuah identifies a first-person singular human subject who ate.
Tla in ōnitlacuah specifies a nonspecific nonhuman thing eaten.
Ōahcico has a third-person singular human subject in the stated ‘he arrived’ interpretation.
Both ōnitlacuah and ōahcico are preterit-tense completed events.
Ye establishes that the eating was already complete by the arrival time.
Ye ōnitlacuah in ōahcico. means ‘I had already eaten when he arrived.’
English represents the principal-clause Nahuatl preterit as past perfect in this temporal relation.
The English past-perfect rendering does not reclassify the Nahuatl principal predicate as a distinct Nahuatl past-perfect tense.
In tihuāllāz, ye ōnitlacuah.
In tihuāllāz is a temporal adjunct clause modifying ye ōnitlacuah.
Tihuāllāz has a second-person singular human subject.
Tihuāllāz is morphologically future tense.
In this temporal adjunct, future tihuāllāz is rendered by English present ‘when you come.’
Ōnitlacuah has a first-person singular human subject.
In ōnitlacuah, tla marks a nonspecific nonhuman object eaten by the subject.
Ōnitlacuah is morphologically preterit tense.
Ye contributes the result ‘already’ to the principal clause.
In this temporal construction, preterit ōnitlacuah is rendered by English future perfect ‘I shall have eaten.’
In tihuāllāz, ye ōnitlacuah means ‘when you come, I shall already have eaten.’
Ye ōcuēl nitlacuah in huāllāzqueh. = Already quickly I-have-eaten adjr they-will-come; i.e., I shall already have eaten when they come.
Ye ōcuēl mic in tahciquīuh. = Already quickly he-has-died adjr you-will-come-in-orderto- arrive; i.e., He will already have died when you get here.
In ōcētica micqueh, mochipa tlaōcoxtinemi in centetl. is a witnessed temporal adverbial-clause construction about a paired set.
The adjoined clause identifies one member of the relevant pair as having died.
The principal clause identifies the other member of the pair as the one who continues living.
Mochipa gives the surviving member's mourning state persistent or ‘always’ duration.
Tlaōcoxtinemi predicates continuing life in sadness or mourning of the surviving member.
In ōcētica micqueh has the temporal value ‘when one of them has died.’
Mochipa tlaōcoxtinemi in centetl has the value ‘the other always lives in mourning.’
In ōcētica micqueh, mochipa tlaōcoxtinemi in centetl. means ‘When one of them has died, the other always lives in mourning.’
In ōquicac in iuh tlanōnōtzqueh in tītlantin, cencah momauhtih. is attested with an interlinear analysis and a temporal English translation.
The sentence realizes 'When he heard the messengers report in this manner, he became very afraid.'
The clause unit iuh tlanōnōtzqueh in tītlantin functions as the supplementary object of ōquicac.
The supplementary object clause supplies the nonhuman propositional content cross-referenced by specific object pronoun qui-Ø in ōquicac.
Within the supplementary object clause, in tītlantin identifies the human plural subject of tlanōnōtzqueh as the messengers.
In ōtlathuic, ye nō ceppa huel quicentlāz in toyāōuh means ‘when it had dawned, our foes once again made an assault.’
quicentlāz in the example has a singular subject pronoun.
Supplementary subject toyāōuh in the example also has a singular subject pronoun.
The singular subject forms may be an instance of nonanimation.

A structure of conjunction may be formed at the level of principal clauses.
In principal-clause-level conjunction, the conjuncts are principal clauses.
A structure of conjunction may be formed at the level of adjoined clauses.
In adjoined-clause-level conjunction, the conjuncts are adjoined clauses.
Conjunction may be either additive (English and), alternative (English or), or adversative (English but).
Any of these may be either marked or unmarked.
In marked conjunction, an explicit conjunctor links the conjuncts.
In unmarked conjunction, the linkage is merely implicit [technically, this is called "asyndeton"].
Be alert to the fact that Nahuatl by far prefers unmarked conjunction.

In unmarked conjunction, the content of the combined clauses is sufficient to establish both that they are conjoined and the nature of their conjunction.
The conjuncts may be a pair or a series.
The conjunction may be positive ("and") or negative ("nor").

In construction one, m-o- identifies the human subject as the prospective possessor of a captive.
In construction one, tē- identifies a nonspecific human who is caused to enter the captive relation.
Construction one has the literal result ‘to cause someone to become one's captive.’
Construction one has the practical result ‘to make someone one's captive.’

The captive in construction two is a human referent originally associated with the other human possessor.
Construction two has the literal result ‘to cause oneself to have someone else's captive.’
Construction two has the pragmatic result ‘to let it be known that someone else's captive is one's own.’
The two constructions share one surface stem but differ in participant structure and result.

Tē-(tla-nāmic-ti-ā) is a witnessed first-causative matched-thing verbstem.

The human participant and nonhuman matched thing occupy distinct roles in every result; evidence for exchange does not suppress recompense.
M-o+tē-(nāmic-tiā) is a witnessed second-causative encounter verbstem.

The source verbstem also licenses 'to encounter someone.'

In§ 5.5.2, remark, it was pointed out that tense (a grammatical category) is not the same as time (an existential category).
Section 5.5.2, remark, is cited for the distinction between grammatical tense and existential time.
This is made evident in Nahuatl in the frequent use of a tense morph to refer to a time other than that strictly and narrowly associated with it.
Such nonsystemic usage occurs primarily in situations where a tense morph in one VNC exerts an influence upon that in another (as when, for…
Consequently, such shifts are most frequent in concatenate constructions, although they may occur across sentence boundaries.
Many instances of the nonsystemic use of tense have already been pointed out.
The present tense is among the tenses most frequently affected by nonsystemic time reference.
The preterit tense is among the tenses most frequently affected by nonsystemic time reference.
The future tense is among the tenses most frequently affected by nonsystemic time reference.
